speaker: Michael Truell
title: Michael Truell: How Cursor Builds at the Speed of AI
question: When a fast-growing AI product starts overwhelming its upstream model API providers, what actually solves that scaling bottleneck?
guest: Stressing the API providers was less about being very clever technically to get past that scale, and more a relationship thing. I do not think the API providers really knew what to make of us, because we were four twenty-somethings whose product suddenly comprised a really high double-digit percent of their API revenue, and now they had to make capacity planning and financing decisions to handle the growth under the hood. So a lot of it was forging relationships with people. It was also getting very clever about the fact that you can get API tokens for the same model from many providers—there are token resellers out there. It is strategically helpful to spread usage across multiple providers that have committed contracts, so we got very good at hunting out all the tokens that exist in the world.

points.core: Overcoming upstream API limits depends more on provider relationships than technical cleverness.
points.note: Accept: stating that breaking through provider rate/capacity ceilings is primarily a commercial/executive relationship problem rather than an engineering optimization problem. Do not credit: pure technical advice like prompt caching, batching, or switching to smaller models.

points.core: Becoming a huge share of provider revenue forces upstream capacity planning bottlenecks.
points.note: Accept: explaining that sudden massive demand makes an app a large fraction of a lab's API revenue, forcing the provider into hard GPU capacity allocation or financing decisions. Do not credit: generic statements that "APIs have rate limits."

points.core: Sourcing identical model tokens across multiple resellers unlocks additional committed inference supply.
points.note: Accept: routing the same underlying model across multiple cloud/API resellers or intermediaries with committed capacity contracts to aggregate supply. Do not credit: generic multi-model fallback to completely different models without mentioning multi-provider sourcing of the same model.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
What solves it is a combination of securing guaranteed capacity and reducing how much of it you need, since rate limits at that scale are a supply problem rather than a coding problem.

On the supply side, the fix is negotiating directly with providers: committed-spend contracts, provisioned or reserved throughput, and custom rate limits. Fast-growing products like Cursor have publicly described hitting this wall and resolving it largely through provider relationships plus spreading load across multiple sources of the same model (for example, Anthropic direct, AWS Bedrock, and Google Vertex; or OpenAI direct and Azure). A routing layer with failover and load balancing across those providers and regions turns several limited quotas into one larger pool.

On the demand side, you cut tokens per request: prompt caching, routing easy tasks to smaller or cheaper models, batching non-urgent work, and trimming context. Many companies also train or fine-tune their own models for high-volume, narrow tasks (autocomplete, apply-edits) and run them on dedicated inference, reserving frontier APIs for the hard requests.

Finally, queueing, backoff, and per-user limits or usage-based pricing smooth peaks, but they manage the shortage rather than remove it.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Solving upstream model API bottlenecks requires moving beyond single-endpoint rate limits through multi-provider orchestration, demand reduction, and workload specialization. Immediate relief comes from placing an AI gateway in front of inference calls to pool quotas across multiple regions and cloud hosts—combining direct provider APIs with AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Azure—while purchasing provisioned throughput for predictable baseline traffic and bursting onto pay-as-you-go tiers.

Alongside wider routing, teams shrink raw token consumption per request using prompt prefix caching, semantic caching, stricter context pruning, and asynchronous batch queues that smooth out non-interactive traffic spikes. Structural leverage comes from model cascading: routing high-frequency tasks like classification, extraction, or autocomplete to smaller, faster models so scarce frontier capacity is reserved for hard reasoning. At true breakout scale, products move their hottest paths off shared APIs altogether, serving fine-tuned or custom distilled models on dedicated GPU clusters where they directly control continuous batching, speculative decoding, and hardware utilization.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Usually it's capacity engineering plus diversification. No single trick fixes it.

Start with the cheap fixes. Cache prompts and responses, batch work that isn't urgent, trim context, and send routine requests to smaller, faster models. Keep frontier models for the hard cases. That often cuts upstream load a lot. Wrap all of it in a gateway that does queueing, backoff, prioritization and graceful degradation, so a spike slows things down instead of causing outages.

Next, stop depending on one shared rate-limited endpoint. Spread traffic across several providers and cloud resellers, such as Anthropic directly, AWS Bedrock, Google Vertex and Azure, with automatic failover. Then negotiate enterprise agreements for reserved or provisioned throughput, which gives you guaranteed capacity instead of best-effort quotas.

At large scale, the lasting fix is owning part of the stack. Fast-growing companies like Cursor have trained their own models for high-volume tasks such as autocomplete and run them on GPUs they control. They keep calling outside APIs only where frontier quality matters. That cuts both the dependency and the cost.

Underneath all of this, the real constraint is GPU supply, so long-term capacity contracts matter as much as good code.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Solving an upstream model API bottleneck usually takes a combination of securing dedicated capacity, spreading load, and reducing how much work hits the heaviest models. The most immediate fix is moving off shared pay-as-you-go rate limits onto provisioned throughput or enterprise capacity commitments, while distributing requests across multiple regions, deployments, and fallback providers through a routing gateway so no single quota caps traffic.

Equally important is cutting unnecessary token volume at the source. High-growth teams introduce model routing—sending simple or high-frequency tasks to smaller, faster models and reserving frontier models for complex queries—alongside prompt caching, tighter context windows, and asynchronous batching for non-interactive jobs. For bursty traffic, request queuing, rate-limit-aware retries, and graceful degradation prevent spikes from cascading into outages.

Once volume becomes large and predictable enough, the lasting solution for core workloads is often moving part of the stack to dedicated or self-hosted inference running fine-tuned open-weights models on reserved GPUs, giving the team direct control over throughput, latency, and scaling.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The bottleneck is solved when you have enough usable inference capacity to meet peak demand. Measure what’s saturating—requests per minute, tokens per minute, or concurrent requests—then raise that specific limit or buy reserved throughput. If one provider can’t supply enough capacity, spread traffic across providers or deployments with independent capacity, and route simpler tasks to smaller models. At sustained volume, running some models yourself can make sense if you can provision and operate the GPUs.

Caching repeated work, trimming prompts, and capping output length reduce the capacity you need. Queues and backpressure absorb short bursts and prevent retry storms. If demand consistently exceeds what your providers can serve, the durable fix is more capacity, less inference work per request, or both.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
What solves the bottleneck is more inference capacity, less work per request, or both. First, distinguish a rate limit from a capacity shortage. If the provider has spare capacity and your account is hitting its quota, a higher limit can solve the problem. If the provider is saturated, you need additional serving capacity, whether the provider provisions it for you, you route some traffic to another provider with spare capacity, or you serve a suitable model yourself.

You can also reduce demand by caching reusable answers, shortening prompts and outputs, or routing simpler tasks to a smaller model. Queues can absorb brief spikes, but if requests keep arriving faster than they can be served, the queue keeps growing. For sustained growth, the system has to process work at least as fast as it arrives.
